category.title: Computational Geometry
category.description: Geometric primitives, line-segment intersections, convex hulls, polygon operations, and geometric sweeping.

algorithms.title: Orientation / Cross Product
algorithms.summary: Find whether three points make a left turn, right turn, or are on the same line.
explanation: Take three points A, B and C.
Imagine going from A to B and then from B to C.
If C is on the left side, the result is positive.
If C is on the right side, the result is negative.
If all three points are on the same line, the result is zero.
This is one of the most important building blocks of Computational Geometry.

traceSteps: 2 is positive, so C is on the left side of AB.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines the direction of three points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use it whenever you need left/right turn or point-side information.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Convex Hull, segment intersection, polygon algorithms and many geometry problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only a few arithmetic operations are required.

algorithms.title: Distance Between Two Points
algorithms.summary: Find the straight-line distance between two points.
explanation: For points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2), calculate dx and dy.
Use the Pythagorean theorem.
Distance = sqrt(dx² + dy²).
Usually compare squared distances when the actual distance is not required.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the distance between two points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use it for closest/farthest points, circles and geometric comparisons.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Closest Pair, circle problems, nearest point problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Distance between two points needs only constant-time arithmetic.

algorithms.title: Squared Distance
algorithms.summary: Compare distances without calculating square roots.
explanation: Sometimes we only need to know which point is closer.
Square root is unnecessary for comparison.
Use dx² + dy² instead.
The point with smaller squared distance is also the point with smaller actual distance.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Efficiently compares geometric distances.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Whenever only comparison is required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Closest point, nearest neighbor and K closest problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoiding sqrt makes the calculation simpler and faster.

codeTemplates.code:
def squared_distance(a, b):
    dx = a[0] - b[0]
    dy = a[1] - b[1]
    return dx * dx + dy * dy

print(squared_distance((3, 4), (0, 0)))

algorithms.title: Collinearity Check
algorithms.summary: Check whether multiple points lie on the same straight line.
explanation: Three points are collinear when their cross product is zero.
For many points, compare every point with the first two points.
This avoids floating-point slope calculations.
Cross product is safer than comparing decimal slopes.

traceSteps: Therefore all three lie on the same line.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether points lie on one straight line.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use it when slope or straight-line alignment is involved.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Uses integer arithmetic and avoids division.

algorithms.title: Point on Line Segment
algorithms.summary: Check whether a point lies exactly on a line segment.
explanation: First check whether the three points are collinear.
Then check whether the point is inside the rectangle formed by the segment endpoints.
Both conditions must be true.
Being on the infinite line is not enough; the point must also be between the endpoints.

traceSteps: A, P and B are collinear.
Therefore P is on segment AB.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether a point belongs to a finite segment.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use it in segment intersection and polygon boundary checks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Requires only constant-time calculations.

codeTemplates.code:
def on_segment(a, b, p):
    cross = ((b[0]-a[0])*(p[1]-a[1])
             - (b[1]-a[1])*(p[0]-a[0]))

    if cross != 0:
        return False

    return (min(a[0], b[0]) <= p[0] <= max(a[0], b[0]) and
            min(a[1], b[1]) <= p[1] <= max(a[1], b[1]))

algorithms.title: Point in Triangle
algorithms.summary: Check whether a point lies inside or on the boundary of a triangle.
explanation: Take triangle ABC and point P.
Calculate orientation of ABP, BCP and CAP.
If all orientations have the same sign, P is inside the triangle.
Boundary points can also be accepted depending on the problem.

traceSteps: P is on the same side of AB as C.
P is on the same side of BC as A.
P is on the same side of CA as B.
Therefore P is inside the triangle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines whether a point belongs to a triangle.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use it for triangle containment problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only three orientation checks are needed.

algorithms.title: Polygon Area - Shoelace Formula
algorithms.summary: Find the area of a polygon using its vertices.
explanation: Write all polygon points in clockwise or counter-clockwise order.
Multiply x of one point with y of the next point.
Subtract the reverse products.
Add everything and divide the absolute value by 2.
This is called the Shoelace Formula because the multiplication pattern looks like shoelaces.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Calculates polygon area.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when polygon vertices are given in order.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Polygon geometry and computational geometry problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every vertex is processed once.

codeTemplates.code:
def polygon_area(points):
    total = 0
    n = len(points)

    for i in range(n):
        x1, y1 = points[i]
        x2, y2 = points[(i + 1) % n]
        total += x1 * y2 - y1 * x2

    return abs(total) / 2

print(polygon_area([(0,0),(2,0),(2,2),(0,2)]))

algorithms.title: Polygon Perimeter
algorithms.summary: Find the total boundary length of a polygon.
explanation: A polygon consists of multiple line segments.
Calculate the distance between every pair of consecutive vertices.
Also connect the last point back to the first point.
Add all these distances.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Calculates polygon boundary length.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when polygon vertices are given.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each edge is processed exactly once.

codeTemplates.code:
import math

def perimeter(points):
    ans = 0
    n = len(points)

    for i in range(n):
        a = points[i]
        b = points[(i + 1) % n]
        ans += math.hypot(a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1])

    return ans

algorithms.title: Point in Polygon - Ray Casting
algorithms.summary: Check whether a point is inside an arbitrary polygon.
explanation: Imagine shooting a horizontal ray from the point towards the right.
Count how many polygon edges the ray crosses.
Odd number of crossings means the point is inside.
Even number means the point is outside.
This is called the Ray Casting or Even-Odd rule.

traceSteps: Shoot a ray from (2,2) to the right.
The ray crosses the right boundary once.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether a point is inside a polygon.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for arbitrary, possibly concave polygons.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Maps, collision detection and geographical systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only one pass through polygon edges is needed.

algorithms.title: Line Segment Intersection
algorithms.summary: Determine whether two line segments intersect.
explanation: Take segments AB and CD.
Use orientation to find which side each endpoint is on.
Normally, AB and CD intersect when the endpoints lie on opposite sides.
Special handling is required when points are collinear.
This is a very common geometry building block.

traceSteps: AB and C/D are on opposite sides.
CD and A/B are also on opposite sides.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks whether two finite line segments meet.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for collision and crossing problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Maps, graphics, collision detection and sweep line algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time orientation tests solve two segments.

algorithms.title: Line-Line Intersection
algorithms.summary: Find the intersection point of two non-parallel lines.
explanation: Represent each line using two points.
Convert the two lines into equations.
Solve the two equations together.
If the determinant is zero, the lines are parallel or coincident.
Unlike segment intersection, this considers infinite lines.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds where two infinite lines meet.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when actual intersection coordinates are required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Geometry, ray tracing and line arrangement problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Two linear equations can be solved in constant time.

codeTemplates.code:
def line_intersection(a,b,c,d):
    x1,y1=a; x2,y2=b
    x3,y3=c; x4,y4=d

    den=(x1-x2)*(y3-y4)-(y1-y2)*(x3-x4)
    if den == 0:
        return None

    px=((x1*y2-y1*x2)*(x3-x4)-(x1-x2)*(x3*y4-y3*x4))/den
    py=((x1*y2-y1*x2)*(y3-y4)-(y1-y2)*(x3*y4-y3*x4))/den
    return px,py

algorithms.title: Convex Hull - Graham Scan
algorithms.summary: Find the smallest convex polygon containing all given points.
explanation: Imagine putting a rubber band around all points.
The points touched by the rubber band form the convex hull.
Choose the lowest point first.
Sort the other points by angle.
Use a stack and orientation to remove points that create a right turn.
The remaining points form the convex hull.

traceSteps: The four corner points form the outside boundary.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the outer boundary of a set of points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when you need the smallest convex polygon containing points.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Geographic mapping, collision detection and many geometry problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by a linear scan.

algorithms.title: Convex Hull - Monotonic Chain
algorithms.summary: Build a convex hull by constructing lower and upper boundaries.
explanation: Sort all points by x and then y.
Build the lower hull from left to right.
Build the upper hull from right to left.
Use cross product to remove points that make the wrong turn.
Join the two hulls.

traceSteps: The center point is not part of the outer boundary.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the convex hull of points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when you want a simple and robust convex hull implementation.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Most competitive programming convex hull problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting dominates the complexity.

algorithms.title: Check Polygon Convexity
algorithms.summary: Check whether every angle of a polygon bends in the same direction.
explanation: A convex polygon always turns in the same direction while walking around its boundary.
Calculate the cross product for every three consecutive points.
All non-zero cross products should have the same sign.
If the sign changes, the polygon is concave.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines whether a polygon is convex.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use before applying algorithms that require convex polygons.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each vertex is checked once.

algorithms.title: Closest Pair of Points - Brute Force
algorithms.summary: Find the two closest points by checking every pair.
explanation: Take every pair of points.
Calculate their squared distance.
Keep the smallest distance.
This is simple but becomes slow for a large number of points.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the closest pair of points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for small input sizes or as a simple baseline.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: It is simple but not optimal for large n.

algorithms.title: Closest Pair of Points - Divide and Conquer
algorithms.summary: Find the closest pair of points efficiently using divide and conquer.
explanation: Sort points by x-coordinate.
Split the points into left and right halves.
Find the closest pair in each half.
Only points close to the middle line can create a better pair across the halves.
Check only a small number of points in the middle strip.
This reduces the complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n).

exampleTrace.input: Several points spread on a plane
traceSteps: Build a narrow strip around the middle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the closest two points efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when n is large and O(n²) is too slow.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Divide and conquer reduces pair comparisons dramatically.

algorithms.title: Farthest Pair of Points
algorithms.summary: Find the maximum distance between any two points using convex hull and rotating calipers.
explanation: The farthest pair must lie on the convex hull.
First construct the convex hull.
Interior points cannot be part of the farthest pair.
Then use rotating calipers to efficiently check opposite hull points.
This avoids checking every pair.

traceSteps: All four corners belong to the hull.
This is larger than side distance² = 4.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the two farthest points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for large point sets.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Convex hull plus calipers avoids O(n²) pair checking.

codeTemplates.code:
def farthest_pair(points):
    # Simple baseline after hull construction.
    # For very large hulls, use rotating calipers.
    hull = sorted(set(points))
    best = 0

    for i in range(len(hull)):
        for j in range(i+1,len(hull)):
            dx=hull[i][0]-hull[j][0]
            dy=hull[i][1]-hull[j][1]
            best=max(best,dx*dx+dy*dy)

    return best

algorithms.title: Rotating Calipers
algorithms.summary: Efficiently solve distance and diameter problems on convex polygons.
explanation: Imagine placing two parallel lines around a convex polygon.
Rotate the two lines around the polygon.
At every position, maintain the points farthest apart.
This lets us find the polygon diameter without checking every pair.
It is normally used after computing a convex hull.

traceSteps: The maximum distance found is the diameter.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Solves maximum-distance and antipodal-pair problems efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use on convex polygons after convex hull.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Polygon diameter, width and distance problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids quadratic pair checking.

codeTemplates.code:
def area2(a,b,c):
    return abs((b[0]-a[0])*(c[1]-a[1]) -
               (b[1]-a[1])*(c[0]-a[0]))

algorithms.title: Distance from Point to Line
algorithms.summary: Find the shortest perpendicular distance from a point to an infinite line.
explanation: For line Ax + By + C = 0 and point (x,y), use the standard distance formula.
Distance = |Ax + By + C| / sqrt(A²+B²).
The numerator tells how far the point is from satisfying the line equation.
The denominator normalizes the line direction.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds perpendicular distance to a line.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use in geometry distance problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Collision detection, projections and line geometry.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time formula.

algorithms.title: Distance from Point to Segment
algorithms.summary: Find the shortest distance between a point and a finite line segment.
explanation: Project the point onto the infinite line containing the segment.
If the projection falls inside the segment, use the perpendicular distance.
Otherwise the closest point is one of the two endpoints.
This handles both cases.

traceSteps: Projection of P onto the line is (2,0).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds shortest distance from point to finite segment.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for collision and nearest-edge problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time projection calculation.

algorithms.title: Point and Circle Relation
algorithms.summary: Determine whether a point is inside, on, or outside a circle.
explanation: Calculate squared distance from the center to the point.
Compare it with r².
If distance² < r², the point is inside.
If distance² = r², the point is on the circle.
If distance² > r², the point is outside.

traceSteps: Therefore the point is on the circle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines the position of a point relative to a circle.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for containment and collision checks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Uses constant-time squared-distance comparison.

codeTemplates.code:
def point_circle_relation(center, r, p):
    dx=p[0]-center[0]
    dy=p[1]-center[1]
    d2=dx*dx+dy*dy

    if d2 < r*r: return 'inside'
    if d2 > r*r: return 'outside'
    return 'on circle'

algorithms.title: Circle-Line Intersection
algorithms.summary: Determine whether a line intersects a circle and how many intersection points exist.
explanation: Find the perpendicular distance from the circle center to the line.
Compare this distance with the radius.
Distance greater than radius means no intersection.
Equal means the line touches the circle at one point.
Smaller means the line crosses the circle at two points.

traceSteps: Distance from center to y=3 is 3.
Therefore the line passes through the circle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines line-circle intersection count.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for geometric collision and intersection problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only a distance comparison is required.

codeTemplates.code:
def circle_line_intersections(cx,cy,r,A,B,C):
    d=abs(A*cx+B*cy+C)/(A*A+B*B)**0.5
    if d > r: return 0
    if abs(d-r) < 1e-9: return 1
    return 2

print(circle_line_intersections(0,0,5,0,1,-3))

algorithms.title: Circle-Circle Intersection
algorithms.summary: Determine how two circles intersect.
explanation: Find the distance d between the two centers.
Compare d with r1+r2 and |r1-r2|.
If d is too large, circles are separate.
If d equals the sum of radii, they touch externally.
If d equals the radius difference, they touch internally.
Otherwise they normally intersect at two points.

traceSteps: Therefore the circles intersect at two points.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines the relationship between two circles.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when circle intersection information is needed.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only center distance and radii are needed.

codeTemplates.code:
import math

def circle_relation(c1,r1,c2,r2):
    d=math.hypot(c1[0]-c2[0],c1[1]-c2[1])
    if d > r1+r2: return 'separate'
    if d < abs(r1-r2): return 'one inside another'
    if math.isclose(d,r1+r2) or math.isclose(d,abs(r1-r2)):
        return 'touching'
    return 'two intersections'

algorithms.title: Triangle Area Using Cross Product
algorithms.summary: Calculate triangle area directly from three coordinates.
explanation: The absolute value of the cross product gives twice the triangle area.
So area = |cross| / 2.
This avoids calculating heights manually.
It works for any triangle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds area of a triangle from coordinates.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when triangle vertices are given.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time calculation.

codeTemplates.code:
def triangle_area(a,b,c):
    cross=(b[0]-a[0])*(c[1]-a[1])-(b[1]-a[1])*(c[0]-a[0])
    return abs(cross)/2

print(triangle_area((0,0),(4,0),(0,3)))

algorithms.title: Triangle Area - Heron's Formula
algorithms.summary: Find triangle area when its three side lengths are known.
explanation: First calculate the semi-perimeter s = (a+b+c)/2.
Then use area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)).
This is useful when coordinates are not given.
The triangle inequality must be satisfied.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds triangle area from side lengths.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when only three sides are available.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time formula.

algorithms.title: Polygon Centroid
algorithms.summary: Find the geometric center of a simple polygon.
explanation: The centroid is the balance point of a polygon.
It is calculated using the cross product of every consecutive edge.
The signed area is used as part of the formula.
For a rectangle, the centroid is simply its center.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the balance point of a polygon.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for polygon center calculations.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Every edge is processed once.

codeTemplates.code:
def polygon_centroid(p):
    area2=0
    cx=cy=0
    n=len(p)

    for i in range(n):
        x1,y1=p[i]
        x2,y2=p[(i+1)%n]
        c=x1*y2-x2*y1
        area2+=c
        cx+=(x1+x2)*c
        cy+=(y1+y2)*c

    return cx/(3*area2), cy/(3*area2)

algorithms.title: Point in Convex Polygon
algorithms.summary: Check whether a point belongs to a convex polygon using binary search.
explanation: For a convex polygon, choose one fixed vertex.
The polygon can be divided into triangles using that vertex.
Binary search identifies the triangle containing the query point.
Then perform a simple triangle check.
This improves the usual O(n) scan to O(log n).

traceSteps: Binary search finds the sector containing the point.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers point-inside-convex-polygon queries quickly.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when there are many point queries against the same convex polygon.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Binary search reduces query time to O(log n).

codeTemplates.code:
def inside_convex_polygon(polygon, p):
    # Simple O(n) version for clarity.
    # Binary-search optimization is used when many queries exist.
    n=len(polygon)
    sign=[]

    for i in range(n):
        a=polygon[i]
        b=polygon[(i+1)%n]
        c=(b[0]-a[0])*(p[1]-a[1])-(b[1]-a[1])*(p[0]-a[0])
        sign.append(c)

    return all(x>=0 for x in sign) or all(x<=0 for x in sign)

algorithms.title: Bounding Box
algorithms.summary: Find the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing all points.
explanation: Find minimum x and maximum x.
Find minimum y and maximum y.
These four values define the bounding rectangle.
The rectangle sides stay parallel to the x and y axes.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for spatial filtering and quick collision checks.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Graphics, GIS, spatial indexing and geometry.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: One pass through all points.

algorithms.title: Rectangle Intersection
algorithms.summary: Check whether two axis-aligned rectangles overlap.
explanation: Represent each rectangle using left, bottom, right and top.
If one rectangle is completely to the left, they do not overlap.
If one is completely above or below, they do not overlap.
Otherwise they overlap.

traceSteps: R2 starts before R1 ends on x-axis.
R2 starts before R1 ends on y-axis.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks overlap between axis-aligned rectangles.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for rectangular collision problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Games, UI layout and spatial algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only a few comparisons are required.

codeTemplates.code:
def rectangles_overlap(a,b):
    # (left,bottom,right,top)
    return not (a[2] <= b[0] or b[2] <= a[0] or
                a[3] <= b[1] or b[3] <= a[1])

algorithms.title: Circle-Rectangle Intersection
algorithms.summary: Check whether a circle intersects an axis-aligned rectangle.
explanation: Find the point on the rectangle closest to the circle center.
Clamp the circle center's x and y coordinates to the rectangle.
Calculate distance from the center to this closest point.
If the distance is at most the radius, they intersect.

traceSteps: Closest rectangle point to center is (3,3).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Checks circle-rectangle collision.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for axis-aligned rectangular collision.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time calculation.

codeTemplates.code:
def circle_rect_intersect(cx,cy,r,left,bottom,right,top):
    x=max(left,min(cx,right))
    y=max(bottom,min(cy,top))
    dx=cx-x
    dy=cy-y
    return dx*dx+dy*dy <= r*r

algorithms.title: Sweep Line Algorithm
algorithms.summary: Process geometric objects from left to right instead of checking every pair.
explanation: Imagine a vertical line moving from left to right.
Only objects currently touching the sweep line are active.
When an object starts, add it.
When it ends, remove it.
Check only relevant active objects.
This turns many O(n²) geometry problems into O(n log n) solutions.

traceSteps: Sort all segment start/end events by x.
Move the sweep line from left to right.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Efficiently processes large sets of geometric objects.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when geometry objects can be ordered along one axis.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Segment intersections, rectangle union and skyline problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids comparing every object with every other object.

codeTemplates.code:
def sweep_events(intervals):
    events=[]

    for left,right in intervals:
        events.append((left,1))
        events.append((right,-1))

    events.sort()
    active=0
    maximum=0

    for x,delta in events:
        active+=delta
        maximum=max(maximum,active)

    return maximum

algorithms.title: Coordinate Compression
algorithms.summary: Convert very large coordinate values into small consecutive indices.
explanation: Sometimes coordinates can be extremely large, such as 1,000,000,000.
But only a small number of coordinates actually appear.
Sort the unique coordinates.
Replace each coordinate with its index.
This makes grid and sweep-line problems much easier to process.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Reduces huge coordinate ranges to manageable indices.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when coordinates are large but the number of unique values is small.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Grid geometry, sweep line and range problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Allows arrays to replace huge coordinate spaces.

algorithms.title: Point Side of a Line / Half Plane
algorithms.summary: Determine which side of a directed line a point lies on.
explanation: A directed line divides the plane into two sides.
Use the cross product of the line direction and point direction.
Positive means one side.
Negative means the other side.
Zero means the point lies directly on the line.

traceSteps: Therefore P is on the left side.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines the side of a line containing a point.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use in convexity, clipping and half-plane problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time cross-product test.

codeTemplates.code:
def side_of_line(a,b,p):
    c=(b[0]-a[0])*(p[1]-a[1])-(b[1]-a[1])*(p[0]-a[0])
    if c>0: return 'left'
    if c<0: return 'right'
    return 'on line'

algorithms.title: Line Equation from Two Points
algorithms.summary: Represent a line using the equation Ax + By + C = 0.
explanation: Two points uniquely determine a line.
Using Ax + By + C = 0 avoids special handling for vertical lines.
For points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2), coefficients can be built directly.
This representation is useful in intersection and distance calculations.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Creates a mathematical representation of a line.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when many line operations are required.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The representation works for both normal and vertical lines.

codeTemplates.code:
def line_from_points(p1,p2):
    x1,y1=p1
    x2,y2=p2
    A=y1-y2
    B=x2-x1
    C=x1*y2-x2*y1
    return A,B,C

print(line_from_points((0,0),(2,2)))

algorithms.title: Circumcenter of Triangle
algorithms.summary: Find the center of the circle passing through all three triangle vertices.
explanation: Every triangle has a unique circumcircle unless the triangle is degenerate.
The circumcenter is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.
Instead of constructing the bisectors explicitly, solve the equations directly.
The resulting point is equally distant from all three vertices.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the center of a triangle's circumcircle.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when a circle through three points is needed.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Only a constant number of equations are solved.

def circumcenter(a,b,c):
    ax,ay=a; bx,by=b; cx,cy=c
    d=2*(ax*(by-cy)+bx*(cy-ay)+cx*(ay-by))

    ux=((ax*ax+ay*ay)*(by-cy)+
        (bx*bx+by*by)*(cy-ay)+
        (cx*cx+cy*cy)*(ay-by))/d

    uy=((ax*ax+ay*ay)*(cx-bx)+
        (bx*bx+by*by)*(ax-cx)+
        (cx*cx+cy*cy)*(bx-ax))/d

    return ux,uy

algorithms.title: Incenter of Triangle
algorithms.summary: Find the center of the circle that touches all three sides of a triangle.
explanation: The incenter is the intersection of the three angle bisectors.
It can also be calculated using side lengths as weights.
If side lengths opposite A, B and C are a, b and c, then the incenter is a weighted average of the vertices.
It is always inside the triangle.

traceSteps: All three angle bisectors meet at the same central point.
Because the triangle is symmetric, this point is also the centroid.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the center of the inscribed circle.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when distances to all three sides are equal.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Triangle geometry and advanced computational geometry.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Constant-time weighted-average calculation.

import math

def incenter(A,B,C):
    a=math.dist(B,C)
    b=math.dist(A,C)
    c=math.dist(A,B)
    s=a+b+c

    return ((a*A[0]+b*B[0]+c*C[0])/s,
            (a*A[1]+b*B[1]+c*C[1])/s)

algorithms.title: Tangent to a Circle
algorithms.summary: Find or reason about tangent lines from a point to a circle.
explanation: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point.
The radius to the tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent line.
If a point is outside the circle, normally two tangents can be drawn.
If the point is on the circle, there is one tangent.
If the point is inside, no real tangent exists.

traceSteps: Distance from center to point is 5.
An outside point has two tangent lines to the circle.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines tangent possibilities between a point and circle.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use in circle geometry and visibility problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: The basic classification requires only one distance comparison.

import math

def tangent_count(center,r,p):
    d=math.hypot(p[0]-center[0],p[1]-center[1])
    if d < r: return 0
    if math.isclose(d,r): return 1
    return 2

algorithms.title: Polygon Triangulation
algorithms.summary: Understand how a simple polygon can be divided into triangles.
explanation: Any simple polygon with n vertices can be divided into n-2 triangles.
For a convex polygon, diagonals from one vertex can make this very easy.
For example, a quadrilateral needs 2 triangles.
Triangulation is an important foundation for more advanced geometry algorithms.

traceSteps: The diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Divides a polygon into simpler triangle pieces.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when triangle-based calculations are easier.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Rendering, mesh generation and polygon algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: A polygon always requires exactly n-2 triangles.

algorithms.title: Minkowski Sum
algorithms.summary: Combine two convex polygons by adding every point of one polygon to every point of the other.
explanation: For sets A and B, the Minkowski sum contains every point a+b.
For convex polygons, the result is also convex.
Instead of trying every pair of points, merge polygon edges by their direction.
This is similar to merging two sorted lists.
It is useful for collision and configuration-space problems.

traceSteps: Merge edge directions from both polygons.
Add the chosen edge to the result.
The resulting boundary is the Minkowski sum.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines two convex shapes into one convex shape.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use in collision and configuration-space geometry.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Robotics, collision detection and computational geometry.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Convex polygon edges can be merged linearly after ordering.

algorithms.title: Rectangle/Polygon Union Concept
algorithms.summary: Calculate the combined covered area of multiple geometric objects without double-counting overlap.
explanation: If two rectangles overlap, simply adding their areas counts the overlap twice.
Sweep-line algorithms process the rectangles from left to right.
At each x-coordinate, maintain the total covered y-length.
Multiply the covered y-length by the x-distance to get the added area.
This technique can be extended to more complex union-area problems.

traceSteps: Create left and right edge events.
Multiply by the current x gap.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds area covered by multiple objects.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when overlapping regions must not be counted twice.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Rectangle union, maps and computational geometry.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sweep line avoids explicitly processing every tiny coordinate cell.

algorithms.title: Half-Plane Intersection
algorithms.summary: Find the common region satisfying many linear half-plane constraints.
explanation: Every line divides the plane into two sides.
A half-plane keeps only one of those sides.
Intersecting many half-planes gives a feasible polygonal region.
The common region can be found using sorted boundary lines and a deque.
This is an advanced computational geometry technique.

traceSteps: Keep the right side of x=0.
Keep the upper side of y=0.
Keep the left side of x=4.
Keep the lower side of y=4.
Their common region is a square.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the common feasible region of linear constraints.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use in advanced geometric constraint problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorted half-planes can be processed efficiently.

algorithms.title: Voronoi Diagram
algorithms.summary: Divide the plane into regions based on the nearest point.
explanation: Suppose several shops are placed on a map.
Every location belongs to the shop that is closest to it.
The regions created by this rule form a Voronoi diagram.
The boundary between two regions contains points equally distant from two sites.
The full algorithm is advanced, but the idea is very important.

traceSteps: A point at x=2 has equal distance from both shops.
Points left of x=2 are closer to the first shop.
Points right of x=2 are closer to the second shop.
Therefore the dividing boundary is x=2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Divides space according to nearest sites.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for nearest-location and spatial partitioning problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Maps, facility planning, robotics and GIS.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Advanced algorithms construct the complete diagram efficiently.

algorithms.title: Delaunay Triangulation
algorithms.summary: Create a triangulation where no point lies inside the circumcircle of any triangle.
explanation: Delaunay triangulation connects points into triangles.
A key property is that the circumcircle of every triangle contains no other input point in its interior.
It tends to avoid extremely skinny triangles.
It is closely related to the Voronoi diagram.
Implementations are advanced and usually rely on robust geometric predicates.

traceSteps: A square can be divided using either diagonal.
Both possible triangulations have valid empty circumcircles.
The resulting triangles form a Delaunay triangulation.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Builds a high-quality triangulation of points.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when a point set needs to become a triangle mesh.
wAnswers.whereUsed: 3D graphics, terrain modeling, GIS and finite-element methods.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Efficient implementations can construct it in O(n log n).

algorithms.title: Lattice Points and Pick's Theorem
algorithms.summary: Count integer-coordinate points inside and on the boundary of a lattice polygon.
explanation: A lattice point has integer x and y coordinates.
For a lattice polygon, Pick's theorem says A = I + B/2 - 1.
A is the polygon area.
I is the number of interior lattice points.
B is the number of boundary lattice points.
Boundary points on an edge can be counted using gcd(|dx|,|dy|).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Counts integer points inside lattice polygons.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when polygon coordinates are integers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Area and boundary counts can be computed in O(n).
